meta.notes: Scope: primary ICP is US dental practices (5-50 staff); home-service trades and Indian clinics covered only by a few items. Most quantitative missed-call figures come from vendor-authored or vendor-hosted pages (Dental Economics piece by an AI-phone vendor developer, StealthAgents, ServiceMag/ServiceForge, Swiss Monkey, eesel); they are flagged as such in statements. The only independent dental dial-out study found is UK 2011 (44%). No primary ADA/peer-reviewed missed-call data was found. Reddit is not fetchable; two r/AI_Agents threads were read through a public snapshot mirror (reddit.sentinel-team.org). Unfetchable (not cited): groupdentistrynow, dentaltown (verification wall), Jobber community (403), Orrick FCC note (robots), ACHR News (robots), ambitionbox (robots), ruby.com (403). FCC 2024 TCPA ruling on AI voices (relevant to outbound reminder calls) was found in search but not cited because the fetchable pages were blocked. Founder-listed vendors Hello22, LuMay, Vapi, Synthflow and Bland were not researched individually (no evidence items); Retell, Arini, Weave, ServiceTitan, Smith.ai, Dentina, Viva AI, Edesy, CallMissed and Swiss Monkey were. Prospects: 20 US dental practices from their own sites (one via a chamber of commerce member directory). Most team pages give first names only; no emails were collected. No company-specific problem evidence (e.g., job posts about missed calls) was found for prospects; technology fit is 0 for all since no site names its PMS.

summary.statement: Vendor-cited benchmarks put dental missed-call rates at roughly 30-38% during business hours, and one cited analysis of 4,280 calls across 26 practices found 38% unanswered.
An independent but old (2011, UK) dial-out study found 44% of calls to dental practices did not reach a person.
For home services, CallRail's benchmark is much lower (14%), while health care is 32%; Invoca-based figures cite 27% for home services.
Not every missed call is a lost booking (spam, repeats, vendors, callbacks), so raw miss rates overstate the opportunity.
Consumer survey data cited for home services: 66% hang up when a call is not answered and 51% stop after contacting one provider.
Practitioners and anecdotes describe callers moving to the next business that answers.

A survey commissioned by a human-answering firm says about a third of callers would hang up on an AI bot, and many patients prefer online self-scheduling, so not all missed callers would be recovered by a voice agent.
No dental-specific primary data on what patients do after reaching voicemail was found.
US dental AI receptionists integrate with Dentrix, Eaglesoft and Open Dental; Weave books directly into only four PMSs and captures requests elsewhere.

Incumbent platforms bundle the capability: Weave's AI receptionist is available to all dental practices and ServiceTitan ships a built-in voice agent that books jobs and aims to replace answering services.
Practice-level expectations for integration were not found in first-person sources.
Dental practices face staffing shortages (62% of dentists named it the top 2025 challenge), including hard-to-fill front-desk roles.
Hiring more staff or basic answering services are described as giving only marginal relief for peak, lunch and after-hours coverage.
AI receptionists themselves struggle with triage, insurance verification, complex reschedules and emergencies, and need a human escalation path.

Published estimates are models, not measurements: $100k-$200k+ a year for a mid-size dental practice, about $1,200 per missed home-services call, and about $16k/month exposure for a 1,000-call/month home-services firm.
Vendor case studies report recovered bookings (e.g., 330 new-patient appointments in 12 months at a one-provider office; 21% more booked jobs at a ServiceTitan customer).
US dental AI receptionists are priced at about $149-$239/month for small practices and $300-$700 for 4-6 chair practices; Dentina and Viva AI publish $299-$349/month.
Alternatives: Smith.ai AI answering at $150/month for 75 calls or human answering from $300/month for 30 calls; a remote human front-office service at $399-$599/month plus hourly fees.
In India, voice agents are already sold at Rs 4-6 per minute, and a starting receptionist earns about Rs 17k-45k a month.
No evidence was found of what individual practices currently spend on call handling.

new_unknowns.question: Will dental practices already on Weave (or another phone/PMS platform with a bundled AI receptionist) pay for a separate vertical voice agent, and what would make them switch?
In India, do clinics and diagnostic labs get most bookings by phone or by WhatsApp, and would they pay Rs 2,999+/month for a voice agent?

evidence.title: The economics of missed calls: Quantifying revenue loss in dental practices
evidence.quote: Industry benchmarks indicate that dental practices miss 30–38% of incoming calls during business hours.
evidence.statement: A Dental Economics article (written by a developer at an AI phone vendor) cites industry benchmarks of 30-38% of dental calls missed during business hours.

evidence.title: The economics of missed calls: Quantifying revenue loss in dental practices
evidence.quote: For a typical midsized practice with three to six operatories and 60–200 calls per day, receiving 300–500 incoming calls per month, a 35% miss rate means 105–175 unanswered calls monthly. … the true annual impact for many practices easily reaches $100,000–$200,000 or more.
evidence.statement: The same article models 105-175 unanswered calls a month for a mid-size practice and an annual impact of $100k-$200k+; a model built on assumptions, not measured loss.

evidence.title: The economics of missed calls: Quantifying revenue loss in dental practices
evidence.quote: Many owners try solving the issue by hiring additional staff or using basic answering services. While these approaches provide marginal relief, they frequently fail to deliver consistent coverage during peak hours, lunch breaks, or after hours.
evidence.statement: Current fixes (more staff, basic answering services) are described as giving only marginal relief for peak, lunch and after-hours coverage.

evidence.title: 44 per cent of phone calls fail to reach practice team - Dentistry.co.uk
evidence.quote: Researchers discovered that of the 3,557 dial-outs made over a 128-hour period, they reached 718 answer machines, 630 busy signals and 202 no answers, which equates to a staggering 44% of all attempted calls.
evidence.statement: An older (2011, UK) independent dial-out study found 44% of calls to dental practices hit an answering machine, busy signal or no answer.

evidence.title: Home Services Missed Call Revenue Statistics 2026
evidence.quote: CallRail reported that home services businesses missed 14% of calls in its January 2025 small-business benchmark. … placed the home services missed-call rate at 14%, behind health care at 32% and legal services at 28%.
evidence.statement: CallRail's benchmark puts home-services missed calls at 14% but health care at 32%: the miss rate is much lower for home services than the idea assumes, and higher for health care.

evidence.title: Home Services Missed Call Revenue Statistics 2026
evidence.quote: A missed call is not automatically a lost job. It may be spam, a repeat caller, a vendor, or a customer who leaves a voicemail and accepts a callback.
evidence.statement: Missed calls overstate lost bookings: many are spam, repeats, vendors, or callers who accept a callback.
